 How to ride in the rain and finish wanting to do it all over again
 Training 
 13/11/26 07:00 
 Migue A. 
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 Whatsapp 
 Email 
 When the rainy season arrives, many cyclists put their bikes away and wait for sunnier days. However, riding in the rain can be a unique experience : landscapes change, sounds fade away and pedaling becomes almost therapeutic.
 11 tips for riding in the rain: the art of enjoying the ride while everyone else stays home
 Advertising 
 All you need is a little preparation, the right clothing and a healthy dose of caution. Here’s a complete guide to riding your bike in the rain, from what to wear to how to look after your bike when you get home. 
 Follow Brújula Bike on Google 
 1. The goal isn't to stay dry, it's to stay comfortable
 The key to enjoying a rainy ride isn't staying completely dry, which is almost impossible, but staying comfortable and warm. Choose technical cycling clothing and avoid materials such as cotton, which absorbs moisture and makes you feel cold.

 A waterproof jacket is your best ally : Invest in a good waterproof, breathable jacket. Models featuring Gore-Tex or other membranes combine water protection with excellent ventilation, preventing that sauna-like effect. Look for a jacket with a double zipper, a dropped rear hem and sealed seams. Reflective details are an added bonus, as visibility is essential on gray days.
 Shorts or tights, depending on the temperature : Not every rainy day is cold. If temperatures are mild, you can wear cycling shorts and apply a thin layer of oil or cream to your legs to help water run off . On colder days, opt for thermal tights or long cycling shorts with a water-repellent treatment, which also offer protection from the wind.
 Base layers that manage moisture : A merino wool or technical fabric base layer helps keep your skin dry by wicking away sweat, even when you get wet. It's essential for retaining body heat and preventing chills.
 Advertising 
 2. Accessories make all the difference
 The body loses a lot of heat through its extremities, so your hands, feet and head need special attention.
 Waterproof gloves : They help maintain a firm grip and keep your fingers warm. Look for models with a thermal lining and silicone palms.
 Overshoes or waterproof footwear : Wet feet can ruin any ride. Neoprene or silicone overshoes are an effective solution. If you don't have any, a plastic bag fitted snugly underneath your overshoes can save the day. 
 Advertising 
 Cap or helmet liner : A waterproof or thermal helmet liner worn underneath your helmet helps keep water from getting through the vents and retains body heat.
 Clear or photochromic glasses : They protect your eyes from water, wind and road debris. Lenses with a hydrophobic coating help keep your vision clear.
 Waterproof neck warmer or buff : It keeps water from running down your neck and provides protection from the wind.
 Pogačar winning with a buff, leg warmers and overshoes. 
 3. You may not like them, but they're simple, cheap and highly effective
 Fenders are one of the most underrated accessories , yet they're among the things that can make the biggest difference when riding in wet conditions.
 They prevent water and dirt from the road splashing onto your bike and clothing. There are foldable versions that attach under the saddle in seconds, as well as rigid models that offer better protection for longer rides or regular use. Your drivetrain, your legs and the rider behind you will thank you.
 4. You may not need new ones if you set up your current ones properly
 Advertising 
 Tires and brakes are two of the bike components that deserve the most attention.
 Lower your tire pressure slightly : Reducing pressure by around 0.5–1 bar improves grip and increases the contact patch, both on asphalt and off-road. Don't go too low, though, or you'll increase the risk of punctures.
 Check the tread and wear : On the road, a smooth tire does not pose an aquaplaning risk , but on trails or gravel, a little tread or texture helps clear water and mud.
 Look after your brakes : Stopping distances increase in the rain, especially with rim brakes. Brake smoothly and anticipate corners and descents. Disc brakes offer greater stopping power, but they also need a moment to clear the water before they bite properly. After every wet ride, check your brake pads and rims: water accelerates wear.
 5. Improve your visibility and make sure others can see you
 Rain reduces visibility for both cyclists and drivers. That's why you should always use front and rear lights, even during the day. 
 A flashing mode helps you stand out without dazzling other road users. Adding reflective details to your clothing, helmet or bike is a simple investment in safety.
 6. Adjust your riding technique
 Riding in the rain is not the same as riding in dry conditions. Technique and attitude make all the difference.
 Avoid sudden turns and hard braking. Ride smoothly, anticipating corners and obstacles.
 Stay off painted road markings, metal covers and drainage grates. When wet, they can be as slippery as ice.
 Be wary of puddles. They can hide potholes, gravel or sharp edges.
 Take smooth lines and look further ahead than usual. Anticipation is essential when grip is limited.
 Adjust your pace. If it's raining heavily or traffic is busy, prioritize safety over speed.
 7. Have a plan B and, if possible, ride with someone
 Riding with someone makes a route safer and more enjoyable. Having company can also motivate you to get out even when the weather is bad.
 If you're riding alone, plan a route with loops close to home or easy exit points . That way, you can get back quickly if the rain gets heavier or the temperature drops too much.
 8. Post-ride care is almost as important as preparation
 Post-ride maintenance is just as important as getting ready beforehand. Water mixed with dust and mud can shorten the lifespan of your drivetrain and bearings. 
 Quick but effective cleaning: As soon as you get home, rinse your bike with clean water and wipe it down with a damp cloth. Don't use a pressure washer. Remove the mud before it dries and clean the drivetrain with degreaser. 
 Dry and lubricate: Once the bike is clean, dry it thoroughly with paper towels or a dry cloth. Apply wet-condition lubricant , designed for wet conditions: it stands up to rain better and protects the chain against rust. If you use wax, you can reapply it every few days during periods of heavy rain.
 Look after electronic components : On e-bikes and bikes with electronic groupsets, don't use pressurized water. Clean connectors with a soft brush and dry them carefully. You can also protect them with a little dielectric grease or a waterproof cover if you expect prolonged exposure to rain.
 Van der Poel in the Roubaix showers.
 9. If your jacket isn't doing its job anymore, you may be able to restore it
 Technical clothing needs special care to retain its performance. Wash waterproof garments with products specifically designed for technical fabrics and avoid fabric softener. From time to time, restore the DWR (Durable Water Repellent) finish with a spray-on or wash-in water-repellent treatment . Clean your glasses by immersing them in water without rubbing the lenses, and let your shoes dry at room temperature with paper stuffed inside. Never place them near a direct heat source.
 10. It rains outside the car, too
 If you need to transport your bike by car on rainy days, use waterproof covers and check the most exposed areas afterward, such as the chain, battery and electrical connections.
 If possible, transport the bike inside the vehicle to avoid direct exposure to water and dirt.
 11. The ride ends with a hot shower
 After a rainy ride, your body can cool down quickly. Take a warm or hot shower and change into dry clothes straight away. If your shoes are soaked, stuff them with newspaper to speed up the drying process.
 Only then will you realize how rewarding riding in the rain can be: the feeling of having overcome your own reluctance and the bad weather is priceless.
 Conclusion: rain isn't the enemy; it's an ally for cyclists who are prepared
 With the right gear, a little planning and some maintenance, riding in the rain can become one of the most enjoyable experiences of the year.
 The sound of raindrops on your helmet, the smell of wet earth and the quiet of empty roads are rewards that only cyclists willing to brave bad weather get to experience.
 So next time you see gray skies, don't put your bike away. Get it ready, protect it and enjoy the ride.
